subject: large sample data(e.g., 1e6) leads to more non-convergence errors than small sample(e.g., 1e3)

messages.author: 8ef7077ff1e0d030
messages.subject: large sample data(e.g., 1e6) leads to more non-convergence errors than small sample(e.g., 1e3)
parts:
Dear all,

I was trying to fit a SEM model to a dataset generated by mvrnorm(m = 0). I've created a large sample dataset (n= 1e6) and then run the model using SEM in lavaan 0.6-3.

> sigma
y1 y2 y3 y4 x1 x2
y1 12.2700 5.640000 7.499000 5.705100 -4.2000 -2.10000
y2 5.6400 6.730000 4.754250 5.378825 -3.1500 -1.57500
y3 7.4990 4.754250 14.724175 9.201757 -5.5650 -2.78250
y4 5.7051 5.378825 9.201758 11.281582 -5.0085 -2.50425
x1 -4.2000 -3.150000 -5.565000 -5.008500 10.0000 3.50000
x2 -2.1000 -1.575000 -2.782500 -2.504250 3.5000 4.25000

set.seed(12479)
y <- MASS::mvrnorm(1e6, rep(0, 6), sigma)

model1 <- '
# measurement model
xi1 =~ 1*x1 + x2
eta1 =~ 1*y1 + y2
eta2 =~ 1*y3 + y4
# regresssions
eta1 ~ xi1
eta2 ~ xi1 + eta1
# estimator covariances
y1 ~~ y3
y2 ~~ y4'

fit1 <- lavaan::sem(model1, data = y)

I had no problem analyzing the data at first. However, when I try to do the replications, soon after a few trial, this error message appears:

Warning message:
In lavaan::lavaan(model = model1, data = y, model.type = "sem", :
lavaan WARNING: the optimizer warns that a solution has NOT been found!

however, when I tried the same procedure using smaller samples (e.g., n = 1e3), I never ran into this error message, at least until 800 replications. I wonder why these things happen because I thought large sample data yield more stable model fit results.

I used the function below to do the replications:

get_data <- function(model, n, ...){
y <- MASS::mvrnorm(n, rep(0, 6), sigma) # rep(mu = 0, n = 6)
fit <- lavaan::sem(model, data = y)
h <- as.data.frame(as.list(lavaan::fitmeasures(fit)))
return(h)
}

nrep <- 800
set.seed(12479)

w4 <- vector("list", nrep)
for (i in 1:nrep) {
w4[[i]] <- get_data(model1, 1e6)
}

I'd appreciate any idea.

Thanks,
Tom

The last two lines are the problem: they make the model non-identified.
The larger the sample size, the easier this is detected.

Thank you for answering my question! I didn't realize the problem was about model identification. In fact, I still do not understand why it is unidentified :( 
(My knowledge in SEM is somewhat limited). 

Could you give little more explanation for why the model is unidentified? I thought a model is identified when 2 conditions are met (# free parameters is less than or equal to the number of observations & every latent variable must have a scale). I would appreciate if you could enlighten me on this point.

Thanks,
Tom

messages.subject: Re: large sample data(e.g., 1e6) leads to more non-convergence errors than small sample(e.g., 1e3)
parts:
"Identification" means slightly different things in different communities.
     A solution is "identified" if the available information leads to one unique best set of estimates, given your choice of estimator (Maximum Likelihood, OLS, etc.). These models imply a structure for the covariance matrix of the observed variables. You can take the unique elements of the sample-based covariance matrix as a set of "knowns," and then attempt to solve for the unknown free parameter estimates. For simple models, you might attempt this algebraicly, though the problem quickly becomes complicated.
     Still, identification requires one best solution for each free parameter in the model. If you use an element of the covariance matrix to solve for one parameter, you cannot use the same piece of information to solve for another parameter. That is the problem with the free residua covariances in your model. With only 2 observed variables per factor, and relations between the factors already saturated, there is very little information left in the covariance matrix for estimating the free residual covariances. In particular, the single covariance between the two indicators of a single factor is not enough to estimate all free parameters associated with each factor, so information must be "borrowed" from elsewhere in the covariance matrix. But that elsewhere is exactly where w would find the information we need to estimate the residual covariances. Having non-negative degrees is freedom is not enough to ensure identification--that is a necessary but not sufficient condition.
--Ed Rigdon
